Psychosis in an Adult: Rule Out a Cause, Then Time It

How long, and only during mood episodes?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Hospitalize first if dangerous or unable to meet basic needs.

Then rule out a drug or medical cause:

  • Urine toxicology
  • Chemistry and glucose
  • TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone)

Then time the psychosis against the gates:

  • Brief psychotic disorder 1 day to under 1 month
  • Schizophreniform disorder 1 to under 6 months
  • Schizophrenia 6 months or more

One or more delusions for 1 month or more, with Criterion A never met, is delusional disorder.

Psychosis only during mood episodes is a mood disorder with psychotic features.

Diagnosis
Criterion A (schizophrenia) Symptoms – 2 or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized or catatonic behavior, negative symptoms · Core – at least 1 is delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech
Management and treatment
Management ladder: schizophrenia spectrum
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineAntipsychotic; hospitalize if dangerous or unable to meet basic needsNo response after an adequate trial (4 to 6 weeks)
Second trialA different antipsychotic; long-acting injectable if nonadherent2 or more adequate trials fail, adherence confirmed
Treatment resistantClozapine, with ANC (absolute neutrophil count) monitoringTop rung
By diagnosis Brief psychotic disorder – supervision and support; a short antipsychotic course if needed, and hospitalization by severity · Delusional disorder – antipsychotic plus psychotherapy
Practice
  1. 24-year-old man, previously well; for 3 months he has: believed neighbors implanted a tracker in his tooth heard voices commenting on everything he does stopped attending classes No episodes of depressed or elevated mood Urine toxicology negative · flat affect → Schizophreniform disorder → a delusion plus prominent voices for at least 1 month and under 6 months
  2. 26-year-old man; for 9 months he has: heard voices believed television hosts send him coded messages lost his job, rarely speaks, stopped bathing No episodes of depressed or elevated mood Vital signs normal · urine toxicology negative · flat affect → Schizophrenia → Criterion A symptoms with functional decline for 6 months or more
  3. 46-year-old woman; for 4 months she has: written daily letters to a news anchor she has never met been certain he loves her Works full time and runs her household; no hallucinations; mood normal Vital signs normal · laboratory studies normal → Delusional disorder → an erotomanic delusion for at least 1 month, with functioning intact and no other psychotic or mood symptoms
  4. 34-year-old woman with 1 year of insulting voices and belief coworkers are poisoning her two depressive episodes (4 and 3 months): low mood, anhedonia, insomnia, guilt, poor focus voices and belief persist 4 weeks after mood normalized Toxicology negative · euthymic → Schizoaffective disorder → Criterion A concurrent with major depressive episodes, 2 weeks or more of delusions and voices without a mood episode, and mood episodes for most of the illness
  5. 29-year-old man with 1 week of euphoria: 2-hour nights, rapid talk, his savings spent believing God chose him to rule the world Similar week 2 years ago; beliefs stopped when mood settled; none between episodes Vital signs normal · toxicology negative → Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features → the psychosis occurs only during the manic episode
  6. 22-year-old man with 2 days of believing federal agents are following him smoked methamphetamine daily for 3 days barely slept No psychiatric history HR 96/min · BP 128/80 mm Hg · oriented to person, place and time → Substance-induced psychotic disorder → the delusion began during stimulant intoxication; timing ties it to the drug
  7. 31-year-old woman with 5 days of: believing the government hacked her phone hearing whispers at night No psychiatric history; neurologic examination normal T 37.0 C · HR 88/min · chemistry panel and TSH normal → Urine toxicology screen → the first-line test still missing after chemistry and TSH; a negative screen lowers suspicion of a drug cause; imaging needs a neurologic finding or history; lumbar puncture needs fever, meningismus or delirium
  8. 40-year-old man with 10 days of believing his coworkers are poisoning his food yesterday he bought a knife to confront them No psychiatric history Vital signs normal · urine toxicology negative · oriented to person, place and time → Hospitalization and an antipsychotic → likely harm to others: admit first, whatever the duration; involuntarily if he refuses and no less restrictive option is safe
  9. 33-year-old man treated for schizophrenia for 6 years still hears voices daily after adequate trials of risperidone, then olanzapine adherence confirmed by pill counts No suicidal or homicidal ideation Vital signs normal · flat affect → Clozapine → 2 or more failed adequate trials with documented adherence define treatment resistance
How NBME framed it: question 1

52-year-old man brought by police for strange behavior after an arrest for disturbing his neighbors for 6 months: aggressively handing out leaflets for the New Age healing business he runs from home claims special abilities to cure all physical and mental ailments very upset; sure the police and the physician are plotting against him and his business “I really have special powers; I can heal everyone in the waiting room” Denies past psychiatric problems, depression, elevated mood or hearing voices; sleeps 6 to 8 hours Examination normal · laboratory studies normal

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Bipolar disorder: grandiose claims; but no low or high mood, and normal sleep.
  • Brief psychotic disorder: an acute presentation after an arrest; but it lasts under 1 month, and his delusion has lasted 6.
  • Schizoaffective disorder: a persecutory delusion; but no mood episode and no second Criterion A symptom.
  • Schizophrenia: a fixed persecutory delusion; but it needs a second Criterion A symptom, and delusions are his only symptom.

Down to two: delusional disorder or schizophrenia. Delusional disorder: delusions alone (grandiose and persecutory) for 6 months; no voices, mood episode or disorganization; sleep and labs normal. (NBME says no hallucinations at all; current criteria allow minor ones tied to the delusion.)

How NBME framed it: question 2

37-year-old man with odd experiences that began 2 weeks ago, after he was fired instead of promoted a guard watched him clear his desk and walked him out six drinks at a bar over 4 hours; felt the patrons knew, were watching and talking about him next morning still felt it; closed the curtains; believed television hosts mocked him over that week a man’s voice called him a failure who would amount to nothing; went out only for food, in dark glasses to avoid recognition everything resolved by the end of the week No serious illness or medications; 2 to 3 beers nightly; marijuana once a month Examination normal · no hallucinations now · logical, goal-directed thinking · alert and oriented to person, place and time

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Adjustment disorder: a clear stressor; but psychotic symptoms would be atypical.
  • Delusional disorder: paranoid beliefs; but it needs 1 month or more, and his lasted a week.
  • Posttraumatic stress disorder: a distressing event; but job loss is not life-threatening, and it needs intrusions and over 1 month.
  • Schizophreniform disorder: delusions and a voice; but it needs 1 to 6 months.
  • Substance-induced psychotic disorder: six drinks and monthly cannabis; but alcohol rarely causes psychosis directly, and his cannabis use is occasional.

Down to two: brief psychotic disorder or delusional disorder. Brief psychotic disorder: paranoid delusions and a voice after a stressor, gone within a week, well under 1 month.

Pairs with Bipolar disorder: psychosis only during mania? Delirium: psychosis with a clouded, fluctuating sensorium?
Transferable rule

Rule out a cause, then ask how long the psychosis has lasted and whether it occurs only during mood episodes.

edits.html:
Bipolar Disorder: Rule Out a Cause, Time the Episode, Then Treat

Mania or hypomania, and what to start or stop?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Hospitalize when needed to prevent harm: mania is an emergency.

Then rule out a drug or medical cause:

  • Urine drug screen
  • TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) and free thyroxine
  • CBC (complete blood count) and basic metabolic panel

Then time the episode:

  • Manic episode 1 week or more, or any length if hospitalized
  • Hypomanic episode 4 days or more in a row
  • Cyclothymic disorder 2 years or more of swings below episode criteria

One manic episode makes bipolar I disorder; psychosis, marked impairment or hospitalization makes an episode manic, never hypomanic.

Treat: stop any antidepressant; start lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic.

Diagnosis
Manic episode criteria Mood – elevated, expansive or irritable mood plus more energy, most of the day, nearly every day · Duration – 1 week or more, or any length if hospitalization is necessary · Symptoms – 3 or more DIGFAST symptoms, 4 if the mood is only irritable · Severity – marked impairment, hospitalization to prevent harm, or psychotic features · Cause – not a substance or medical condition; an episode that outlasts an antidepressant still counts · Mixed features – 3 or more depressive symptoms on most days of the episode
DIGFAST
  • Distractibility – attention too easily drawn to irrelevant stimuli
  • Indiscretion – painful consequences: buying sprees, sexual behaviours, foolish business investments
  • Grandiosity – inflated self-esteem
  • Flight of ideas – thoughts are racing
  • Activity increased – goal-directed, or psychomotor agitation
  • Sleep decreased – feels rested after only 3 hours
  • Talkativeness – pressure to keep talking
Management and treatment
Management ladder: acute manic episode
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineStop antidepressants; lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic, alone or an antipsychotic plus lithium or valproateNo better after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses, adherence and substances checked
Add on or switchAnother first-line agent, added or switchedNo improvement after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses
Severe or resistantElectroconvulsive therapyTop rung
By situation Severe agitation or psychosis – sedating second-generation antipsychotic, sometimes lorazepam; lithium takes 4 to 10 days · Could become pregnant – avoid valproate: teratogenic · After remission – continuous maintenance for years; lithium lowers suicide risk · Bipolar depression – suicide risk first; quetiapine, lithium, lamotrigine or lurasidone; no antidepressant alone
Practice
  1. 31-year-old woman with 5 days of: sleeping 4 hours without fatigue faster speech and three new work projects Coworkers notice; she still meets deadlines; only past episode: major depression 2 years ago Elevated mood · no delusions · toxicology negative · TSH normal → Bipolar II disorder → 4 or more days of symptoms others notice, without marked impairment or psychosis, plus a past major depressive episode
  2. 27-year-old man brought in after walking into highway traffic, laughing 3 days without sleep savings spent on a sailboat; talks without pause Admitted for his own safety; no delusions; no earlier mood episodes Expansive mood · toxicology negative · TSH normal → Bipolar I disorder → hospitalization satisfies both the duration and the severity criteria, so 3 days is enough
  3. 29-year-old man with 9 days of: 3-hour nights, rapid speech, new business plans is certain he can heal the sick with his touch Still works daily; major depressive episode 1 year ago Expansive mood · toxicology negative · TSH normal → Bipolar I disorder → psychotic features make the episode manic by definition, even while he keeps working
  4. 38-year-old woman with 10 days of irritable mood and: 2-hour nights, racing thoughts, nonstop talk $9,000 spent online; stopped going to work most days: crying, calling herself a terrible mother, thoughts of death Past admission for elevated mood Toxicology negative → Bipolar I disorder, manic episode with mixed features → irritable mood with 4 symptoms and marked impairment (stopped going to work) for 10 days, plus 3 or more depressive symptoms on most days; the past admission for elevated mood already makes it bipolar I
  5. 26-year-old woman on sertraline 4 weeks for depression; for 8 days she has: slept 3 hours a night, talked rapidly quit her job to launch three businesses; says she is destined for fame Euphoric mood · HR 92/min · pregnancy test negative → Stop sertraline and start quetiapine → a full manic episode on an antidepressant: stop the antidepressant and start a first-line agent
  6. 33-year-old man found on his apartment roof at night announcing that he can fly 9 days of almost no sleep gave away his car; talks nonstop Refuses admission, saying he has never felt better Expansive mood · toxicology negative → Inpatient psychiatric admission → hospitalization is needed to prevent harm to himself; mania is an emergency; involuntarily if he refuses and no less restrictive option is safe
  7. 29-year-old man in the emergency department shouting threats and throwing chairs at staff a week without sleep; pressured speech believes he is a secret agent chosen to save the world Similar hospitalization 2 years ago Irritable, expansive mood · toxicology negative → Sedating antipsychotic and lorazepam → severe manic psychosis compromising safety needs rapid behavioral control; lithium takes 4 to 10 days
  8. 41-year-old woman hospitalized with elevated mood, no sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech lithium for 16 days, at therapeutic levels for 14 every dose confirmed She is no better Toxicology negative → Add quetiapine to lithium → no improvement after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses with adherence and substance use checked: add on or switch
  9. 24-year-old woman admitted with 10 days of: little sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, reckless spending Elevated mood; no psychotic symptoms; sexually active with inconsistent condom use Pregnancy test negative · TSH normal · toxicology negative → Divalproex → valproate should not be used in a woman of childbearing potential (fetal malformations, impaired intellectual development)
  10. 35-year-old man admitted 4 months ago for a week of euphoria, no sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech euthymic for 3 months on lithium at therapeutic levels asks to stop it now that he feels well BP 120/78 mm Hg → Continue lithium long term → maintenance for all patients with bipolar I disorder, continuous rather than intermittent
  11. 30-year-old woman with 3 weeks of: depressed mood, loss of interest, oversleeping, fatigue, poor concentration Hospitalized 2 years ago for 10 days of euphoria, no sleep, grandiosity and spending; no suicidal thoughts HR 72/min → Sertraline monotherapy → antidepressant monotherapy is not used in bipolar I depression and risks a switch to mania; quetiapine, lithium, lamotrigine or lurasidone is first line
  12. 45-year-old man on lithium for 6 years after two admissions for euphoria, grandiosity and no sleep 2 weeks of depressed mood, insomnia, poor appetite, slowed movements, hopelessness says his family would be better off without him HR 76/min → Assess suicide risk → most suicide deaths in bipolar disorder occur in the depressive phase, so suicide risk comes first
  13. 36-year-old woman with 8 days of: little sleep, restlessness, rapid speech, irritability 4-kg weight loss over 6 weeks; always feels hot Fine tremor of the outstretched hands HR 118/min · toxicology negative → Serum TSH and free thyroxine → weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia and tremor point to hyperthyroidism, a medical cause of these symptoms
How NBME framed it: question 1

24-year-old receptionist at an accounting firm brought in by police cursed at a rental car agent; grew “out of control” when no luxury sports car was available asks for the physician’s number, winks, promises “a good time” and tries a kiss agitated; feels “absolutely fantastic”; loud, rapid speech says she is obviously very rich and the agents will regret delaying her for a television interview Examination normal · urine toxicology negative

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder): hyperactive and impulsive; but ADHD is chronic and in more than one setting, and this is acute.
  • Delusional disorder: a fixed grandiose belief; but delusional disorder excludes mania, and she has it.
  • Histrionic personality disorder: the wink and the attempted kiss; but personality disorders are chronic and pervasive.
  • Schizophrenia: a grandiose delusion; but it sits inside a manic episode (NBME cites missing negative symptoms).

Down to two: bipolar disorder or histrionic personality disorder. Bipolar disorder: the seductiveness sits inside an acute episode of euphoric, irritable mood with rapid speech, overspending and grandiosity. (NBME gives no duration; it reads the severity and psychosis as mania.)

How NBME framed it: question 2

43-year-old man admitted with superficial frostbite of the toes police found him 5 hours earlier walking barefoot in a snowstorm says he is a god who can melt snow and purify the heart knows the date and place asked to recall red, penny, train, he playfully laughs: “color, coin, conveyance” rapid, incessant speech; paces with arms raised, both index fingers aimed upward Normal vital signs and laboratory results

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Brief psychotic disorder: an acute delusion; but his psychosis is secondary to mania.
  • Delirium, alcohol withdrawal: found wandering in the cold; but vital signs are normal and he is fully oriented.
  • Delusional disorder: a fixed delusion; but delusional disorder excludes mania, and he has it.
  • Malingering: an odd, dangerous act; but nobody walks into frostbite for gain, and he has none.
  • Schizoid personality disorder: an odd man; but he is playful and talkative, not detached.
  • Schizophrenia: the god delusion and the posture; but the delusion is part of mania (NBME cites missing negative symptoms).

Down to two: bipolar disorder, manic, or schizophrenia. Bipolar disorder, manic: the god delusion rides on playful, euphoric affect, rapid incessant speech and pacing; NBME also cites no negative symptoms.

Pairs with Psychosis in an Adult: Rule Out a Cause, Then Time It: does the psychosis occur only during a mood episode? The Patient on Lithium: Which Complication, and What to Do: what does maintenance lithium do to the kidney and thyroid? Delirium: Tell It From Dementia and Psychosis, Then Find the Cause: are attention and orientation intact? Part I Thyroid Mimics & Discriminators: is a thyroid cause driving the energy and weight loss?
Transferable rule

Before naming a psychosis or a personality disorder, rule out a drug or thyroid cause, then ask whether the symptoms sit inside a discrete episode of elevated or irritable mood with DIGFAST symptoms; if they do, it is mania, and any antidepressant stops.
